extracted.intended_audience: reporters and city editors covering accidents, fires, and other mishaps for newspapers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for reporters on how to cover wrecks, fires, and other accidents — what facts to gather, how to structure leads, safety and crew procedures, and how to make accident stories human and useful to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covering a wreck — circulate, observe, ask
rubrics_metrics.description: Covering a wreck means circulating, observing, asking; in brief, wearing out shoe leather. The reporter who sits on a rail fence and remarks 'Pretty fair smashup' will write half a column; the one who buzzes around will have three or four columns of copy, every paragraph interesting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be active on scene: move about, canvass, interview, and gather many visual and human details rather than passively watching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include genuine human-interest details
rubrics_metrics.description: Interest, so long as it is genuine. Little value resides in the statement of a fellow who says, 'I was asleep in lower 7 and when I woke up, here I was in the hospital.' Speedy interviewing probably will turn up several human interest stories (examples: a man of seventy-four on his first train ride; a honeymoon couple separated).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek concrete, human anecdotes that illuminate the event; avoid banal or obviously invented quotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mention famous or prominent names
rubrics_metrics.description: Famous or prominent names. One of the men in the smoker was the speaker of the state assembly. He is worth strong mention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give prominence to known figures in the lead or early paragraphs because they make the story more interesting to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report heroism but omit identifications for cowardice
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatic bits as of heroism or cowardice. These will be found only by interviewing, but they give a story humanness as no other material can hope to do. Names and identifications are wanted for the stories of heroism, but they are omitted from accounts of cowardice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify and name those who performed heroic acts; when reporting cowardly acts, avoid identifying individuals (ethical and editorial consideration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect wreck sidelights and small vivid details
rubrics_metrics.description: Wreck sidelights, often of the freak variety. That woman holding a baby lost her shoes during the excitement, but she clung to the vacuum bottle with the milk for the youngster's next feeding. The car they were in is crumpled, twisted steel, but the glass in the bottle didn't break.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for vivid, humanizing small details that make copy memorable and illustrate the scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include statements from responsible railroad/official sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Any explanations or statements issued by responsible railroad men. Probably these will come from the general offices, but occasionally an on-the-spot statement will be made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Get official statements from responsible company or agency representatives and clearly attribute them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report freight cargo and logistical impacts for freight wrecks
rubrics_metrics.description: If the wreck involved a freight train, tell something of its cargo. Two cars of cattle were on their way to a Chicago slaughterhouse and now are sidetracked... Has anyone remembered to water the animals? Two or three cars are tagged as containing perishable goods. Are they shunted to a sidetrack while their cargo rots...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe cargo, perishable concerns, and broader logistical consequences — these details matter to readers and affected parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fire reporting — do not enter burning buildings; position at command post
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the reporter should go depends upon circumstances, but it can be said confidently that inside the burning building isn't one of the places. A dead reporter can't write a fire story. Often the place to be is near the commanding officers of the fire department to whom the captains and lieutenants make their reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize reporter safety and obtain overview information from the 'post of command' where tactics and situation are known; avoid being in dangerous positions for the sake of photos or drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask 'Why?' about firefighting tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: By waiting for a comparatively free moment, the reporter can question the fire executives with fair hope that they will be able and willing to take the time to answer him. 'Why?' is the most important question. 'Why did the firemen break the windows on the north side of the building but not those on the west side?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand and explain the tactical reasons behind actions to make the story informative to readers wondering about visible decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fire story currents — Loss of life and injuries (verify rumors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Loss of life, injuries. Rumors fill the air... The gossips will build a casualty list for a wastebasket fire; the reporter must verify everything he hears or sees about deaths or injuries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully verify casualty information; do not repeat unconfirmed rumors. Prioritize accuracy on life-and-death claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fire story currents — Extent of damage (use conservative figures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent of damage. The property owners are all on hand, and so are the insurance men... The property owners boost their figures... The reporter uses the most conservative figures, for he knows that a fire is unpredictable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Get damage estimates from multiple sources, be skeptical of inflated figures, and prefer conservative, attributable estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fire story currents — Rescues as dramatic human narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Rescues. Almost always these are dramatic and they are probably the most 'human' bits in the story. They permit a narrative chronicling, a welcome respite from the catalog of injuries and damage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gather detailed accounts of rescues — they make compelling narrative elements and illustrate human stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fire story currents — Lives menaced or property threatened
rubrics_metrics.description: Lives menaced or property threatened. Sometimes a fire is more interesting in respect to what it might have done than for what it actually did.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report on potential or near-misses and broader impacts (e.g., interruption of factory work) to show the larger significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fire story currents — Sidelights showing human nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Sidelights. Human nature shows itself during a fire. Close watching and quick interviewing discover many excellent angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe and record human reactions, quirky incidents, and small details that reveal character and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fire story currents — Cause (get expert opinions; acknowledge uncertainty)
rubrics_metrics.description: The cause. The fire chief and the battalion commanders sometimes can tell from the nature of a fire exactly how it started. The causes of other blazes never may be known... The fire department will be very glad to give the reporter its opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report suspected causes with attribution; distinguish between official findings, expert opinion, and public rumor; note when the cause is unknown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid staged or false-dramatic reporter heroics
rubrics_metrics.description: The motion-picture reporter, dashing into the roaring building ahead of the firemen, getting trapped on a roof about to cave in... isn't genuine. Inside the building he would see little... Outside, near the 'post of command'... is his place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist temptation to create dangerous or implausible heroics. Authenticity and safety trump sensationalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stay on scene and follow up; don't underestimate re-ignition
rubrics_metrics.description: Underestimating a fire's tenacity has spoiled many a good story... A reporter who stayed after other reporters went home found the blaze erupted again and that floor collapse killed a dozen men; his paper scooped the town.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain contact and be prepared to return: follow-up reporting can yield major developments that initial accounts miss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop notification channels with fire department/police
rubrics_metrics.description: The tip about a fire comes from either the police or the fire department... In many cities the reporters have a treaty with the fire department to notify the paper of every alarm. In return a couple of copies are dropped each day without charge at fire headquarters. In some larger cities a newspaper has in its office a dial connected with fire headquarters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish reliable channels (agreements, direct lines) to receive timely alerts of alarms and incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crew reporting — assign definite tasks and value teamwork
rubrics_metrics.description: A really bad accident will be covered by an entire crew of reporters... each staff member is given definite work. The youngest reporter seems slighted... He is to walk each street in the business district and count the windows broken... If he fails to follow his assignment, the whole plan for covering the story has gone smash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize scenes with clear roles and communication; even routine or seemingly minor tasks contribute to a complete coverage plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: If you find something unexpected, get it or tell the editor
rubrics_metrics.description: When, following his assignment, he comes upon something unexpected and not in the plans, he either gets the information or finds out where it can be obtained, and speedily informs the city editor or the crew chief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report new leads promptly to allow team adjustments and to prevent missed scoops.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transportation accidents — include legal investigators and coroner findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Accidents of transportation always involve the legal authorities. An airplane accident will be investigated by the Federal and in many instances by the state inspectors... The coroner or medical examiner probably is the best information source as to the legal aspects of fatal accidents... The coroner usually is more talkative and even before he has given his official findings he may summarize his information as to the causes of an accident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and quote the relevant investigating agencies (federal, state, coroner) and note their tentative findings and timelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid cataloging statistics; emphasize persons
rubrics_metrics.description: The ordinary accident story may be one of the most interesting in the paper or one of the flattest. Because the necessary facts are many, inexperienced reporters make their stories drab catalogs of statistics... Then, suddenly alarmed... they attempt to dispel the drabness by tricks of diction and pollute their stories into flashy freaks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance necessary facts with human-interest elements; don't substitute ornate diction for real reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double-barreled approach: combine verified statistics with human impression
rubrics_metrics.description: Yet in making an accident recital interesting, 'impressionism' cannot crowd out the statistical facts. Thus the chronicle must be double barreled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include clear, verified factual data and weave in evocative, human details or narrative to engage readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the five-W lead appropriately but don't overload it
rubrics_metrics.description: The five-W lead, though it should not be used incessantly, often is the best device... This perfectly good summary outlines the event in a single, high-velocity sentence. The full five-W form is workable until its details pile up and become cumbersome. Then, and only then, should it be dropped.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a compact five-W lead for ordinary accidents; avoid cramming too many names/identifiers or complex detail into a single sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'preview' leads — hold some W's for later paragraphs
rubrics_metrics.description: Cut out one, two, or even three of the W's, and hold them until the second paragraph. This gives a 'preview' first paragraph... Using only some of the W's in the lead gives flexibility permitting high emphasis upon any one outstanding news facet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the full five-W lead would be clumsy, lead with the most newsworthy element and expand remaining Ws immediately after.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose lead type to suit the story: name-driven, circumstance-driven, complex, or roundup
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: (1) A newsworthy name and several other names of no especial significance; (2) 'Ordinary' names linked to an unusual circumstance; (3) Circumstances too complex for quick explanation; (4) A combination story rolling several accidents into one account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the lead structure that best conveys what will most interest readers; use rollups for multiple events and characterizing leads for complex incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize How/Why/What more than When/Where in many leads
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'How,' the 'Why,' and the 'What' are the W's that distinguish one accident from another. Accordingly they are emphasized, with 'When' and 'Where' subordinated to a few words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize the elements that make the incident distinct; but adjust prominence when 'When' or 'Where' are immediately useful to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prominence of 'Who' depends on reader familiarity
rubrics_metrics.description: How prominently 'Who' should be in the lead cannot be ruled upon arbitrarily. The better known a name... the higher in the story 'Who' should come... If completing the identification takes the crackle out of the lead, a nameless opening probably is better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put names high when they add immediate interest; avoid clumsy, overloaded identifications that dampen readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Link readers with the news via identification but avoid overloading
rubrics_metrics.description: A lead giving too little 'Who' is compact; adding 'local' or 'high-school' or names helps readers answer 'Did I know him?' But identifying so completely (occupations, family notes, long biographical detail) can swamp action words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide the minimal identifying detail (local, age, school, occupation) that helps readers recognize individuals without burying the core action in exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: For water stories, pin down 'Where' specifically
rubrics_metrics.description: In water stories the 'Where' requires pinning down, since many waters are large enough that an unelaborated mention gives readers a vague concept of the geography. Many readers wish to know 'did it happen near our summer place?' Accordingly the reporter gets high in the story such an elaboration as 'a quarter of a mile offshore from Mallett's Bay on the south side of the lake.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give precise geographic detail for incidents on large bodies of water or places with ambiguous names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fire leads must state if anyone was killed or hurt and convey seriousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The first two requisites of a fire story lead are to tell whether anyone was killed or hurt and then give a definite concept of the seriousness of the blaze. Regardless of how high the property damage and how inconspicuous the one man who was suffocated, loss of life is mentioned before property damage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place human casualties before monetary losses and give readers a clear sense of the blaze's magnitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make property-damage estimates visualizable, not just dollar figures
rubrics_metrics.description: The estimated damage should remain in the lead, but not necessarily at the top. Find an expression that can be more easily visualized than can money... 'Fire that menaced an entire business block' or 'A blaze that roared for five hours' suggest enormity readers can comprehend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate dollar estimates into vivid descriptions (duration, area threatened, iconic buildings affected) so readers grasp scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overwrought, clichéd, or melodramatic phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Striving for vivid phrasings, a reporter wracks the language. He devises wordings so terrible that their only hope for posterity is in the horribles-example list... Or, the reporter rings in a tottering cliche that even the leisurely news writers of 1820 would have rejected as outworn. Examples: 'Belching billows of bilious smoke.' 'The great red demon, Fire... poured his hot, flaming breath.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for vividness without melodrama; avoid hackneyed metaphors and hyperbolic personifications.
